title: Women, integration and Storyville
summary: They discuss women's interest in musicians and how jazz promoted mixing, including Boston's Storyville, where Stewart worked with Tatum.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: How did you -- were women as interested in musicians in those days as they are now, because almost anytime
guys play a date, there's always a lot of women who are interested in musicians.
Yes, I think there was just -- they were very interested in the musicians. Oh, yes.
How did -- because, you know, like one of the reasons why there were problems, like the Storyville in Boston was because there was so much integration going on in Boston --
Right, yes.
-- that they closed Storyville down once because they said it led to too much race-mixing.
Yes.
Because we have a lot of black guys and white girls and stuff (inaudible)... people in Boston (inaudible).

That's right. I remember the Storyville because I worked there with Tatum on one of our -- that was one of our stops on the way. So good old Storyville. And like you say, there was integration, what have you.

Did you find that there was more integration taking place with, you know, I mean, not only socially, but romantically, in the jazz world than in other areas of life that you encountered during those years?
If I look at it real close, I would say yes, sure, because, well, a musician or musicians, they come in contact with the public, you know, and the public, when

they were playing their engagements here and there and other, they come in contact with thousands and thousands of people, you know. I think it was possible that that had a lot to do with integrating contacts and what have you. It played a big part.
Did you find yourself with many women in those days?
At times, sure, yes.

I mean, were you pursued more in certain areas of the country or certain clubs than others that stand out in your mind? Because sometimes, you know, like you go on the road and somebody say, "Man, you know, you get to -- the women in L.A., they really like musicians." You know what I mean, you know what I'm saying? In certain --
In different places, it was moreso. Like you say, L.A., sure, yes. But I played it cool, you might say.
(Laughter.)
You kind of played that down.
Oh, yes.
You didn't get overinvolved.
That's right, sure.
